v.why: Raising a very small learning rate fixes undertraining within 243 epochs, while raising an already large one does not.
Cutting an overly large learning rate restores stable training, giving large gains (e.g. experiments 69, 77, 78).
Deeper networks at a large learning rate diverge more easily (experiments 47, 57, 58 show huge drops).
Strong L2 penalty underfits, so weakening it helps (experiments 6, 7).
Pushing an already strong L2 penalty higher causes underfitting (experiment 14).
Larger batches give less noisy gradients, which stabilizes training at large learning rates (experiments 23, 25, 27).
Narrow networks are capacity-limited, so widening them helps more than widening already wide ones.
Increasing an already large learning rate causes instability (experiments 67, 73, 74).
Shallower networks are easier to keep stable at large learning rates, so removing a layer helps there.
Smaller batches add gradient noise that compounds with a large learning rate and destabilizes training.
